---
title: "Day 23: Exercises — Integrated chemistry"
---

Connect structure, stereochemistry, reaction mechanisms and experimental evidence in each case.

**Core exercises 1–10:** begin here. **Transfer 11–16:** apply the same ideas to
new cases. **Further checks 17–20:** use these to investigate mistakes and revise.
Allow roughly **2–3 hours** across the unit, with more time for complete mechanism
drawings. Attempt each problem before opening its hint, then compare your reasoning
with the worked explanation.

## Working refresher

Use the same checks on every case: identify functional groups, draw explicit atoms and charges at the changing site, follow electron pairs, and test a proposed structure against observations. In wedge/dash drawings, solid wedge points toward the observer and dashed wedge away. For a tetrahedral centre rank CIP priorities by atomic number, break ties with next attached atoms and treat multiple bonds by duplicated-atom bookkeeping; with priority 4 away, clockwise 1→2→3 is R and anticlockwise S. For the simple C/H/O spectra use DBE=(2C+2−H)/2 and the supplied first-order n +1 rule. Amount=n=m/M; theoretical product comes from balanced limiting extent; apparent yield=100×isolated/theoretical mass. The [local lecture](lec.qmd) provides the chemical drawings used in these exercises.

## 1. Read lactic acid without a pathway

For CH₃CH(OH)COOH, identify both oxygen-containing functional groups, alcohol type and the possible stereocentre. Supply the four groups attached to that centre.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The CH(OH) carbon, rather than the carbonyl carbon, is tetrahedral.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
The molecule has a secondary alcohol and carboxylic acid. CH(OH) bears OH,H,CH₃ and COOH, four different groups, so it is a stereocentre. No metabolic knowledge is needed to infer those features.
:::

## 2. Rank the carbon substituents

At the lactic acid centre, compare COOH with CH₃ using supplied CIP multiple-bond bookkeeping: duplicate a doubly bonded atom in the attached-atom comparison. Give the complete priority order.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The directly attached atoms tie at C; compare their next atoms.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
COOH carbon compares as O,O,O while methyl compares H,H,H, so COOH outranks CH₃. Complete order is OH>COOH>CH₃>H. Atomic identities, not group size or drawn length, determine priority.
:::

## 3. Assign a view with lowest priority away

In a tetrahedral drawing H(4) points away. OH(1) is at upper left, COOH(2) upper right and CH₃(3) lower left. Determine R/S and explain what reverses if H points toward you instead.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Read 1→2→3 with the lowest-priority group away.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
The sequence is clockwise in this stated view, so R. If the same apparent sequence is viewed with H toward the observer, invert the result to S or reorient a model. A page rotation alone does not change configuration.
:::

## 4. Distinguish mirror and rotation

Two lactic-acid drawings have identical connectivity but opposite tetrahedral arrangement at their sole stereocentre. State their relationship and whether R/S predicts the sign of optical rotation.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Configuration and a measured optical property are distinct labels.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
They are enantiomers and cannot be superimposed by rigid rotation. R/S does not determine positive or negative optical rotation; that sign must be measured or otherwise supplied.
:::

## 5. Draw one acid–base mechanism

For lactic acid plus OH⁻, draw removal of the carboxyl OH proton with both curved arrows. Give products and state whether that step inverts the alcohol-bearing centre.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Start an arrow at the base pair and the other at the acid O–H bond.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
CH₃CH(OH)COO⁻ and H₂O form. The proton-transfer step does not break or rearrange the bonds at CH(OH), so it does not itself invert that centre. Other conditions could cause other chemistry, but that is not this drawn event.
:::

## 6. Check atom conservation quantitatively

For CH₃CH(OH)COOH+OH⁻→CH₃CH(OH)COO⁻+H₂O, count C,H,O and total charge on each side. Explain why dropping the water product would fail the audit.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Lactic acid is C₃H₆O₃ and lactate is C₃H₅O₃⁻.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
Each complete side has C₃H₇O₄ and total charge −1. Omitting water loses H₂O from the inventory and hides the proton recipient; electron-flow bookkeeping alone cannot permit atoms to disappear.
:::

## 7. Use a supplied ionisation model

For a dilute monoprotic acid with pKa 3.86, use fraction_Aminus=1/(1+10^(pKa−pH)). Calculate fractions at pH3.86 and 4.86 and interpret the population.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
At one pH unit above pKa the ratio A⁻/HA is 10.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
Fractions are 0.5 and 10/11≈0.909. They describe relative populations of acid and conjugate-base species, not molecules each losing half or 90.9% of a proton.
:::

## 8. Predict oxidation and geometry

Oxidise the secondary alcohol in CH₃CH(OH)COOH to a ketone while retaining the carbon skeleton. Write the product and explain what happens to the original stereocentre.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A secondary alcohol becomes a ketone at its OH-bearing carbon.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
The product is CH₃C(=O)COOH, pyruvic acid. The changing carbon becomes trigonal planar, so the original tetrahedral R/S centre no longer exists.
:::

## 9. Check the oxidation-state change

At the changing carbon of lactic acid assign +1 per C–O bond order,−1 per C–H and 0 per C–C. Compare the ketone product carbonyl.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The alcohol centre has one C–O and one C–H; ketone has C=O and no C–H.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
The alcohol centre is +1−1=0; the ketone carbon is +2. The increase by 2 confirms oxidation. This conclusion does not require adding an oxygen atom to the molecular formula.
:::

## 10. Choose a target ester site

The selected target from lactic acid and ethanol is CH₃CH(OH)COOCH₂CH₃. Identify the functional-group change and state a condition-related limitation of this target drawing.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The drawn secondary OH remains; the carboxylic acid becomes ester.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
Acid-group esterification is the intended net change. The drawing does not guarantee selective reaction under arbitrary conditions, since the starting molecule has more than one reactive oxygen function. Actual conditions and competing pathways must be assessed.
:::

## 11. Track the alcohol oxygen

In standard esterification, ethanol is labelled at oxygen as CH₃CH₂O*H. Write the labelled ethyl-lactate target and identify the two atoms directly bonded to O*.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The incoming alcohol O forms the new bond to acyl carbon.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
CH₃CH(OH)C(=O)O*CH₂CH₃. O* is bonded to the acid-derived carbonyl carbon and the ethyl CH₂ carbon. Atom identities follow the pathway rather than being inferred from final drawing positions.
:::

## 12. Choose addition versus substitution

Compare CH₃CHO and CH₃COOCH₃ reacting with a suitable nucleophile. State the shared first bond changes and the key reason their later pathways can differ.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Both initial attacks move the carbonyl pi pair, but the ester has an oxygen-based substituent at acyl carbon.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
Both form C–Nu and move C=O pi electrons to O. The ester can undergo a viable leaving-group step to restore C=O; ordinary aldehydes lack the corresponding group, since H⁻ is not a normal leaving group here.
:::

## 13. Read amino-acid charges

For H₃N⁺CH(CH₃)COO⁻, identify individual formal charges and net charge. Does net zero make it equivalent to an entirely uncharged hydrocarbon in water?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Sum the charges without deleting their local presence.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
N is +1 and carboxylate −1, net 0. The molecule is zwitterionic and contains strongly polar charged sites, so net neutrality does not make its interactions hydrocarbon-like.
:::

## 14. Predict high-pH deprotonation

Starting from H₃N⁺CH(CH₃)COO⁻, draw OH⁻ accepting one ammonium proton. Give the product formula, N bond count and net charge.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The N–H bonding pair returns to N.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
H₂NCH(CH₃)COO⁻ and water form. N has three bonds and a lone pair, neutral; carboxylate remains −1. Net −1 on each complete side is conserved.
:::

## 15. Assign a complete unknown dataset

U1 has C₄H₈O₂, carbonyl IR without broad OH, proton peaks 1.25 t 3H,2.05 s 3H,4.12 q 2H. Assign CH₃COOCH₂CH₃ and link each observation to a structural part.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Join the ethyl quartet/triplet, then place the acetyl singlet and carbonyl.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
O–CH₂ gives 4.12 q 2H and terminal ethyl CH₃ gives 1.25 t 3H. Acetyl CH₃ gives 2.05 s 3H because adjacent carbonyl C has no H. Ester carbonyl explains IR and lack of acid/alcohol OH; all atoms fit the formula.
:::

## 16. Test a hydroxyketone alternative

For the same U1 dataset, compare CH₃COCH(OH)CH₃. Explain two predicted differences without using filenames or expected reaction products as evidence.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The proposed O-bearing carbon is CH, not CH₂.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
The hydroxyketone predicts an OH-bearing 1H environment and a methyl adjacent to CH, commonly a doublet in the simple model. It also predicts OH functionality. U1 instead has O–CH₂2H quartet and ethyl 3H triplet, favouring the ester among these candidates.
:::

## 17. Calculate yield while stating its assumption

A1:1 teaching reaction has 0.0100 mol limiting reagent, product M180.16 g/mol and isolate 1.70 g. Calculate theoretical mass and apparent yield, then state why neither number proves purity.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Theoretical amount comes from starting reagents; isolated mass enters separately.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
Theoretical mass is 1.8016 g and apparent yield 94.4%. The calculation assumes isolated mass is product; impurities, residual solvent or wrong identity can invalidate that interpretation. Purity requires separate evidence.
:::

## 18. Resolve contradictory observations

A sample gives 94% apparent yield and one TLC spot, but full NMR has an unexpected major signal group. Give a defensible interpretation and two possible explanations without identifying a unique impurity.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A single separation feature can hide co-migration, and mass can include other components.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
The sample may not be pure despite its plausible mass. Residual solvent or another organic component could contribute; incorrect assignment is also possible. Investigate with complete spectral assignments or a discriminating separation rather than ignoring the contradiction.
:::

## 19. Critique a reproducible but invalid calculation

An Rmd file always reproduces 100×isolated_mass/starting_reagent_mass and calls the result percent yield. Explain why reproducibility alone does not make this formula chemically correct.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Mass yield must use theoretical product mass from balanced stoichiometry and molar masses.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
The denominator is generally wrong because starting and product molar masses and coefficients can differ. Correctly compute theoretical product amount from limiting extent, convert using product molar mass, then compare isolated product mass. Repeating an invalid formula is reproducibly wrong.
:::

## 20. Write a final evidence-based conclusion

You have a formula-consistent ester candidate, matching simulated IR/NMR, an apparent 66.6% yield from teaching masses and no actual measured isolate spectra. Write a supported claim, limitation and useful next observation for a real sample.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Keep model demonstration and real measurement separate.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked explanation"}
The supplied simulated evidence supports the ester candidate and the teaching mass calculation gives 66.6% apparent yield under its assumptions. It does not identify or establish purity of a real isolate. Appropriate measured sample spectra and independent purity assessment would test that real-sample claim.
:::
